title: Short Stuff: Simple Spelling Movement
summary: Short Stuff episode on the simplified spelling movement. Josh and Chuck open with a joke about the word "stuff" and introduce the topic of English being hard to spell. They cover Teddy Roosevelt's 1906 executive order adopting simplified spellings for federal documents, the backlash from the press and Congress, and the Simplified Spelling Board founded by Andrew Carnegie, Mark Twain and William James. They discuss earlier advocates Noah Webster and Benjamin Franklin, spelling bees, how spelling changes happen naturally (fish, honor/color), James Ruggles' proposals for "knowed" and "noe", and Edward Ron Thaler's 1970s push tied to literacy and crime. They close with literacy statistics (99 percent basic literacy, 21 percent functional illiteracy) and sponsor and credit mentions.

segments.title: Opening banter and the 1906 spelling push
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about the show name and introduce simplified spelling movements, including Teddy Roosevelt's 1906 interest in the topic and his supporters.

segments.title: Roosevelt's executive order and backlash
segments.summary: Roosevelt ordered federal documents printed with simplified spellings of about 300 words. The press mocked him, and Congress, angry at being sidestepped, pushed a bill citing Webster's dictionary. Webster and Franklin had earlier supported simpler spelling.

segments.title: How tricky English spelling is
segments.summary: Chuck explains that English spelling rules contradict each other, with examples like 'ough' and '-ght', so spellers must memorize words. Josh notes that spelling bees are mostly an English-speaking phenomenon.

segments.title: Spelling bees and natural spelling change
segments.summary: The hosts discuss spelling bee words and their own spelling skills. Josh explains the Simplified Spelling Board aimed to speed up natural spelling change, citing fish (formerly fyshe) and US versus UK spellings like honor and color.

segments.title: James Ruggles and social resistance to phonetic spelling
segments.summary: Josh describes James Ruggles, an Ohio teacher, who proposed spellings such as 'noe' and 'knowed'. Chuck says phonetic forms can make writers look unintelligent, which may explain resistance even from literate reformers like Twain and Carnegie.

segments.title: Revival in the 1970s by Edward Ron Thaler
segments.summary: After the movement faded for decades, Edward Ron Thaler of the American Literacy Council revived it in the 1970s. He linked literacy problems to crime, and the hosts note that computers could convert text to simplified spelling automatically.

segments.title: Literacy statistics and the future of spelling reform
segments.summary: Josh notes a 99 percent basic literacy rate among Americans, versus 21 percent functional illiteracy (about 71 million people). Chuck suggests texting changes spelling on its own, but formal reform is unlikely.

segments.title: Sign-off and credits
segments.summary: Josh thanks sources including History.com, Time, Paleo Future, Smithsonian, and Uncle John's Bathroom Reader. The hosts close the episode and credit the iHeartRadio production.
